section_summary: This section documents Japan’s foreign exchange controls and their effects on payments, imports, diplomatic remittances, and foreign businesses in Japan and China. Two analyses assess Japan’s gold and foreign exchange resources for financing the war in China. Reports from Tsingtao, Shanghai, and Chefoo describe Japanese efforts to control export bills, exchange rates, and currency circulation.

subfiles.title: Maruzen letter on delayed payment for publications
subfiles.about: Maruzen requests more time to pay for books and periodicals while awaiting a Japanese exchange permit.
subfiles.summary: Explains the delayed remittance and requests an extension.

subfiles.title: Reply to Henry A. Barton on Japanese exchange permits
subfiles.from: Maxwell N. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains Japan’s exchange permit process and offers to inquire if payment remains delayed.
subfiles.summary: Describes possible causes of permit delays and says there is no basis to assume Maruzen’s permit will be refused.

subfiles.title: Japanese bank balances in New York
subfiles.about: Japanese New York bank balances fell by about $15 million as Japan shipped gold to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Records Mr. Dietrich’s report of a decline from about $35 million to $20 million.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to frozen American assets in Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a Yokohama despatch on American firms’ frozen assets in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Names Standard Vacuum Oil, Singer, and Ford as affected firms.

subfiles.title: File annotation on quoted Department letter
subfiles.about: Notes that a letter quotes the Department out of context.
subfiles.summary: Warns that the quotation misrepresents the Department’s reply.

subfiles.title: Barton’s acknowledgment of the Department’s reply
subfiles.about: Barton thanks Hamilton and says he may seek help if Maruzen’s payment is further delayed.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges the Department’s view that administrative congestion may explain the delay.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to reported Chrysler credit
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram seeking investigation of a reported Chrysler credit to Japanese automobile companies.
subfiles.summary: Records a Tokyo press report of a $1 million credit.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to proposed yen bloc
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum on Japan’s proposed yen bloc in China and Inner Mongolia.
subfiles.summary: Notes potential diversion of China’s foreign exchange to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to exporter credit warning
subfiles.about: Points to a Hankow telegram about advice to obtain irrevocable letters of credit for exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cites Japanese restrictions on importers’ foreign exchange permits.

subfiles.title: Hankow press report on credits and Japanese exchange controls
subfiles.about: A local paper reports possible British and American credit restrictions and a warning to exporters.
subfiles.summary: Relays a press account linking credit policy, investments in China, and Japanese exchange permit restrictions.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum for analysis of Japan’s external resources
subfiles.about: Forwards Mr. Patton’s assessment of Japan’s end-of-1937 economic position.
subfiles.summary: Introduces an analysis focused on Japan’s external resources.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Foreign Exchange Resources at the End of 1937
subfiles.from: Mr. Patton, Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s gold, overseas balances, and securities available to finance imports and military operations.
subfiles.summary: Estimates realizable foreign exchange resources at roughly $465–500 million, including Bank of Japan gold reserves. It examines trade deficits, gold shipments, foreign securities, and expected import needs. The author concludes that financial strain is substantial but unlikely by itself to force an imminent change in Japan’s objectives in China.

subfiles.title: Foreign exchange arrangement for American film imports
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed arrangement to import American films while deferring dollar payments for three years.
subfiles.summary: The proposed credit arrangement would permit about 60 percent of normal American film imports without supplying exchange for Japan’s essential imports.

subfiles.title: Importation of 200 American Films Before Year-End May Be Permitted
subfiles.about: Reports discussions over limited American film imports and deferred remittance of film receipts.
subfiles.summary: Describes proposed import limits, deposits, and Japanese officials’ views.

subfiles.title: Japanese control of Tsingtao export bills
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese requirement that exporters negotiate bills through the Yokohama Specie Bank.
subfiles.summary: Exporters face an unfavorable official rate and delayed permits; the telegram also notes a reported Chinese exchange control proposal.

subfiles.title: Possible exchange control in Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports a press claim of planned exchange control despite denials by local officials.
subfiles.summary: Connects possible controls with the proposed Japan–Manchukuo–China economic bloc.

subfiles.title: Temporary permission for held Tsingtao exports
subfiles.about: Reports that held shipments may proceed without using the Yokohama Specie Bank.
subfiles.summary: Warns that future export applications will be considered separately.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum for Japan’s foreign exchange position
subfiles.about: Forwards Mr. Patton’s memorandum on Japanese finance.
subfiles.summary: Calls attention to four conclusions developed in the attached memorandum.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Foreign Exchange Position
subfiles.from: Mr. Patton, Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s decision to use Bank of Japan gold reserves for a foreign exchange revolving fund.
subfiles.summary: The transfer of 300 million yen in gold suggests exhaustion of the government gold fund and determination to support the yen. The memorandum examines Japan’s difficulty obtaining commercial credit and its effort to restore exports. It questions how a fund tied to export production could also finance military imports.

subfiles.title: Facilities for remitting official and personal funds abroad
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits diplomatic correspondence on simplified Japanese procedures for remitting funds abroad.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the Belgian Ambassador’s circular and the Japanese Foreign Minister’s reply, with translations.

subfiles.title: Circular Note No. 9
subfiles.from: Baron de Bassompierre, Dean of the Diplomatic Corps
subfiles.about: Shares Japan’s response to a request for simpler diplomatic remittance procedures.
subfiles.summary: Invites colleagues’ views on the apparently satisfactory response.

subfiles.title: Foreign Minister’s reply on diplomatic remittances
subfiles.about: Sets out exemptions and simplified approvals for foreign missions’ official and personal remittances.
subfiles.summary: Official funds may be remitted with quarterly reporting; personal funds may receive longer term authorization. The ministry requests Belgian remittance totals for 1937.

subfiles.title: Translation of Circular Note No. 9
subfiles.from: Baron de Bassompierre, Dean of the Diplomatic Corps
subfiles.about: English translation of the Dean’s circular sharing Japan’s remittance policy.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the inquiry and invites colleagues’ views.

subfiles.title: Translation of the Foreign Minister’s reply
subfiles.about: English translation of the new remittance procedures for foreign missions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Official remittances require quarterly notification rather than prior permission; personal remittances may receive broader authorization. The ministry asks for Belgian totals.

subfiles.title: Instruction concerning circulation of remittance policy
subfiles.about: Assumes the embassy has informed American consular offices of Japan’s new diplomatic remittance policy.
subfiles.summary: References despatch 3126 and the July 16 Foreign Minister’s note.

subfiles.title: Request for updates on exchange restrictions
subfiles.about: Requests continuing reports on exchange restrictions and diplomatic exemptions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges despatch 3126 and forwards related consular telegrams.

subfiles.title: Japanese request for Tsingtao exporters’ contract details
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese request for lists of exporters with outstanding contracts.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin seeks instructions before passing on information collected from American exporters.

subfiles.title: Instruction to protest Japanese demand for exporter information
subfiles.about: Directs the consul to withhold exporters’ information and protest the Japanese request.
subfiles.summary: Exporters may decide individually whether to provide their information.

subfiles.title: Tsingtao protest and blocked peanut oil shipment
subfiles.about: Reports a protest and a lost peanut oil sale after refusal of an export permit.
subfiles.summary: The exporter declined to route its bill through the Yokohama Specie Bank.

subfiles.title: Borden Company’s exposure to Shanghai exchange control
subfiles.doc_type: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum
subfiles.about: Summarizes possible losses to Borden if Shanghai exporters must surrender exchange at the official rate.
subfiles.summary: Notes Borden’s roughly $600,000 in egg product stocks.

subfiles.title: Possible Effects of Controlled Exchange on Shanghai Exports
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Forwards Borden’s concern about possible control of Shanghai export bills.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart considers immediate control unlikely but possible if Japanese authority in Shanghai strengthens.

subfiles.title: Borden Company letter on frozen egg export stocks
subfiles.from: The Borden Company, signed by Thos. H. Pond, Jr.
subfiles.about: Warns that retroactive exchange control could cause major losses on contracted egg exports.
subfiles.summary: Borden estimates a loss of about 40 percent if forced to surrender dollars at the official rate.

subfiles.title: Consulate reply to Borden Company
subfiles.from: R. P. Butrick, for the American Consul General
subfiles.about: Suggests ways for Borden to document its position on cargo exposed to possible exchange control.
subfiles.summary: The consulate has shared Borden’s letter and suggests contacting customs and the Central Bank of China.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese trade in Rio Grande do Sul
subfiles.about: Points to a Porto Alegre despatch on Japanese representatives’ unsuccessful trade efforts.
subfiles.summary: Cites scarce exchange, low offers, and resistance to barter.

subfiles.title: Rieser Company letter on Chefoo currency restrictions
subfiles.from: N. R. Rieser, The Rieser Company
subfiles.about: Reports disruption of American business by Japanese backed currency measures in Chefoo.
subfiles.summary: Encloses a representative’s account of scarce accepted currency and conflicting exchange rates.

subfiles.title: Rothschild’s report on currency conditions in Chefoo
subfiles.about: Describes currency shortages, restricted notes, and barriers to trade in Chefoo.
subfiles.summary: The report says Shanghai issued notes are rejected, while Japanese backed Federal Bank notes have limited acceptance. Northern issued national currency is scarce and is withdrawn from circulation when received by the authorities.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Rieser Company
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the company’s report on currency and exchange conditions in Chefoo.
subfiles.summary: Says the Department is monitoring developments in North China.

subfiles.title: Tsingtao export controls after consular protest
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese refusal to permit some foreign exports unless bills use the official yen exchange rate.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Consul General defends the policy as equal treatment for Japanese exporters. Sokobin describes uneven enforcement and warns that Japanese control over trade and exchange could extend to imports.

subfiles.title: Continuation on Japanese trade control in Tsingtao
subfiles.about: Urges immediate representations in Tokyo over interference with American trade in Tsingtao.
subfiles.summary: Warns that control of imports and exports could establish a Japanese dominated yen bloc.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tsingtao telegrams on export controls
subfiles.about: Restates Sokobin’s account of Japanese export controls and their implications for American trade.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the Japanese Consul General’s position, the differing treatment of exporters, and the consulate’s concern about a yen bloc.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tsingtao despatch 349
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Tsingtao despatch on Japanese pressure to use the Yokohama Specie Bank.
subfiles.summary: Flags losses to exporters and broader implications for foreign trade.

subfiles.title: Japanese Measures to Compel Exporters to Deal with Yokohama Specie Bank
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador, Peiping
subfiles.about: Details Japanese naval measures tying Tsingtao export permits to the Yokohama Specie Bank and its yen rate.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin explains how the bank’s rate could impose large losses on exporters compared with rates available through other banks. He describes Japanese pressure on British banks and the wider effort to connect North China’s currency to the yen. He warns that the policy could sharply curtail foreign trade and might later be imposed through customs.
